subject: Tenant fairness: grace window & deferred bursting amendment

Subject: Questions on queueing & preemption for reserved GPUs

Hi Lauren —

Thanks again for the demo last week. Our infra team has one open question before we sign the reserved GPU addendum: how does Redwood treat tenant fairness when a reserved pool hits transient contention during a regional maintenance event? Specifically:

- Do reserved nodes ever preempt (soft-evict) running requests from other reserved tenants to satisfy higher-priority work?
- Is there a documented grace window (seconds) before preemption that preserves in-flight requests?
- Can we get a temporary burst allowance for traffic spikes (we saw 3x p95 on Black Friday-like tests) and how is that accounted against our commit?

I attached a short traffic sample so you can see our burst shape. We want to avoid surprises: if Redwood will preempt after 5s we need to change our client-side backoff. If you can propose amendment language for the Dedicated SLA that covers a temporary burst token pool and a grace-window for in-flight KV requests, that would be ideal.

Thanks — happy to hop on a 30m call if easier.

Aldo Ramos
Head of ML Infrastructure
Axiom Retail

Hi Aldo —

Appreciate the sample — useful visibility. High level answers up-front:

- Reserved pools do not forcibly terminate in-flight token generation mid-response; we use a conservative "soft-eviction" approach that allows a short grace window to complete current generation steps.
- We can offer a configurable grace window; our standard is 10s for small-token requests but it’s negotiable for enterprise commits.
- We support time-limited burst credits ("burst tokens") that consume a small portion of headroom; they’re chargeable against the commit only after the baseline is exhausted and are visible in the console.

I'm looping in Ben and Rishi to propose precise amendment wording and the operational mechanics. Would you be available 11/12 or 11/13 for a 30m to go over the exact SLA language and a short demo of the burst dashboard?

Next steps: Ben will sketch the amendment, I’ll attach a draft and HubSpot deal link, and Rishi can confirm how preemption looks from a runtime perspective.

— Lauren

From: Ben Carter <ben.carter@redwood.com>
To: Lauren Bishop <lauren.bishop@redwood.com>, Rishi Malhotra <rishi.malhotra@redwood.com>

Subject: Re: Questions on queueing & preemption for reserved GPUs

Lauren / Rishi —

Draft technical summary for the amendment (high level):

1) Grace window: default 10s per request. If a node enters contention due to maintenance or overload, in-flight requests are allowed to complete for up to the configured grace window before any soft-eviction is attempted. This window is configurable per-customer in the Dedicated config up to 30s.

2) Soft-eviction behavior: soft-eviction will: (a) allow current generation to finish up to the grace window, (b) mark request as preemptible for the scheduler and move queued work to other healthy nodes when possible, (c) avoid hard-killing KV cache operations (we persist partial KV to reduce warm-up on re-schedule).

3) Burst tokens: an hourly allotment of burst tokens can be purchased as an addendum (we propose 10% of committed throughput as default). Tokens are first consumed during spikes; if tokens are exhausted we fall back to standard queuing with best-effort routing. Tokens are visible in the Console with an "estimated charge" and are reconciled on a monthly invoice.

4) SLA credits: credits for missed throughput SLOs will scale linearly with minutes of degraded availability above a 1-minute grace for maintenance. If degradation is caused by preemption tied to a customer's own misconfiguration (e.g., runaway job), credits are not applied.

Proposed language (short): "Redwood will not preempt in-flight requests for more than a configurable grace window (default 10s). Customers may purchase hourly burst token allotments to cover transient spikes up to N% above committed baseline. Credits for missed throughput SLOs are calculated per Section X."

I can convert the above into legal-friendly amendment copy. Also attaching a short runbook we reference internally so you can see the operational flow.

— Ben

Hi Aldo —

Thanks for the sample and the question. Based on our internal review we've drafted a short amendment that captures the behavior and gives you a controlled burst mechanism. Key points below; full proposed amendment attached.

Summary (what we propose)
- Grace window: default 10s for in-flight requests; configurable up to 30s via Dedicated config.
- Soft-eviction: in-flight requests will be permitted to finish within the grace window; queued work may be shifted to healthy nodes where capacity allows. Hard termination of in-flight generations will not occur as part of normal preemption.
- Burst tokens: Axiom would get an hourly burst token pool equal to 10% of committed throughput. Tokens are consumed only during above-baseline spikes and are reconciled monthly. We propose a 30-day trial of burst tokens at no incremental charge to validate sizing.
- SLA credits: see Section 3 of the attached amendment for a simple per-minute credit table; credits are excluded for degradation due to customer-caused overload.

Attached: proposed_amendment_v1.pdf (legal-neutral draft) and the traffic sample you sent.

If this looks okay, next steps:
1) We provision a 30-day burst token trial on your Dedicated pool and monitor usage.
2) We finalize amendment language (I can send to legal).
3) DocuSign the addendum and update the HubSpot deal: https://app.hubspot.com/deals/1234567/AXR-2026-118

Are you available for a 30m sync Monday 11/16 or Tuesday 11/17? If so we'll provision the trial immediately after the call.

Best,
Lauren Bishop
